fields.Front: Electric potential difference \(V_b-V_a\) in terms of potential energy
fields.Back: \(V_b-V_a=\dfrac{U_b-U_a}{q}\): potential energy per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C)
fields.SpeakFront: electric potential difference, V b minus V a, in terms of potential energy
fields.SpeakBack: U b minus U a, divided by q; potential energy per unit charge. One volt is one joule per coulomb
fields.Elaboration: Only differences are physical; \(V=0\) can be placed anywhere, like \(U_{grav}=0\).

fields.Front: Potential difference from the electric field: \(V_b-V_a=\,?\)
fields.SpeakFront: potential difference from the electric field, V b minus V a
fields.SpeakBack: minus the line integral from a to b of E dot d l
fields.Elaboration: Follows from \(U_b-U_a=-\int\vec F\cdot d\vec l\) divided by \(q\). The field is conservative, so the path doesn't matter.

fields.SpeakBack: E equals minus the gradient of V; it points toward decreasing potential

fields.Situation: A negative charge moves to a point of lower potential (\(\Delta V<0\)). Does its potential energy rise or fall?
fields.Trap: Assuming a charge always loses potential energy when \(V\) drops. Slide 6's sign table even lists (−)(−) → −.
fields.Fix: \(\Delta U=q\Delta V\): \((-)(-)>0\), so its potential energy rises
fields.Why: Negative charges move on their own toward higher \(V\). "Downhill" means \(\Delta U<0\), not \(\Delta V<0\).
fields.SpeakSituation: a negative charge moves to lower potential. Does its potential energy rise or fall?
fields.SpeakFix: delta U equals q delta V; negative times negative is positive, so its potential energy rises

fields.Front: Why are electric field lines always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces?
fields.Back: Along an equipotential \(dV=-\vec E\cdot d\vec l=0\), so \(\vec E\perp d\vec l\). Equivalently, \(-\nabla V\) is normal to the level sets of \(V\).
fields.SpeakFront: why are electric field lines always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces?
fields.SpeakBack: moving along an equipotential, d V equals minus E dot d l equals zero, so E is perpendicular to the direction of motion; the gradient is normal to level sets
fields.Elaboration: That's also why moving a charge along an equipotential takes no work.

golden.note: The red 'level sets?' guessed right; the card confirms the math behind it.

fields.Front: When finding \(V(r)\) outside a charge, why integrate from \(\infty\) to \(r\)?
fields.Back: Because \(V(\infty)=0\) is the reference: \(V(r)=V(r)-V(\infty)=-\int_\infty^r\vec E\cdot d\vec l\)
fields.SpeakFront: when finding V of r outside a charge, why integrate from infinity to r?
fields.SpeakBack: because the reference is V equals zero at infinity, so V of r equals V of r minus V at infinity, which is minus the integral from infinity to r of E dot d l
fields.Elaboration: The limits encode the reference point. Swap them and you get \(-V\).

golden.note: The slide asks this question itself: a professor's rhetorical question is a free why-card.

review.reason: fine, but maybe asking what to integrate from is better, since thats the thing to recall?

fields.Situation: Finding the potential inside a charged conducting sphere (radius \(r_0\), charge \(Q\))
fields.Fix: \(V=kQ/r_0\) everywhere inside: constant, equal to the surface value
fields.Why: \(\Delta V=-\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l=0\) only says \(V\) doesn't change from the surface inward. Physically, no work is needed to move a charge around inside.
fields.SpeakSituation: finding the potential inside a charged conducting sphere of radius r naught and charge Q
fields.SpeakFix: it is k Q over r naught everywhere inside, constant and equal to the surface value
